name: Video Editing Basics
objectives: Given a short brief and a set of raw clips, organize the footage in a named project folder and set the project's aspect ratio and frame rate to match where the video will play, with every clip easy to find and no clip stretched or cropped by mistake

Using a free video editor, build a rough cut by trimming, splitting and ordering clips on the timeline into a beginning, middle and end, that tells the brief's story in the target length with no dead time
Given a rough cut, add B-roll, cutaways and simple transitions to hide jumps and keep the video moving, using no more than one or two kinds of transition

Given a cut with speech and music, balance the sound levels and add accurate captions and on-screen text, so every word can be heard and read, the meter never hits the top, and all music is used with permission

Given a finished edit, export the video with settings that fit the platform, review it against the brief and write a short portfolio note, so the file plays correctly on the first try and the note names the brief, your role and your tools

chapters.name: Chapter 1: From raw clips to a rough cut

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Read the brief and organize your footage
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write down a brief and set up a named project folder with your clips sorted.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short brief and a set of raw clips, you will organize the footage in a named project folder and set the project's aspect ratio and frame rate to match where the video will play, with every clip easy to find and no clip stretched or cropped by mistake.
Every editing job starts with a brief: a short description of what the video is for. A good brief answers five questions: who will watch it, where it will play (for example YouTube, Instagram Reels, TikTok, a TV in a shop window), how long it should be, what one message it must get across, and when it is due.
Next, organize. Editors lose hours hunting for clips. Make one project folder with a clear name, like "2026-11 Bakery promo". Inside it, make folders for video, audio, music, graphics and exports. Copy your clips in and give the best ones short names, like "oven-closeup" or "owner-interview".
Keep a second copy of your raw clips somewhere else, such as a USB drive or cloud storage. If a phone breaks or a file gets deleted, the job is not lost.
Check permission now, not after you post. Everyone who can be clearly seen or heard should agree to be in the video, and anyone under 18 needs a parent or guardian to agree too.
Step by step:
- Write the brief: audience, platform, length, one message, due date.
- Make a project folder with a clear name and the date.
- Add folders for video, audio, music, graphics and exports.
- Copy your clips in and rename the best ones.
- Back up the raw clips in a second place.
- Check that everyone on camera agreed.
Words to know:
- Brief: a short description of what a video is for: who it is for, where it plays, how long, the message and the due date.
- Footage: the raw video clips you filmed before editing.
- Back up: keep a second copy of your files in another place.
- Client: the person or business you are making the video for.
Try it now: Pick the video you will make for the final task (a team highlight, a shop promo, a job-program story or your own idea). Write a five-line brief on paper. Then make the project folder with its five inside folders, copy in 8 to 15 clips you filmed, and rename the five best ones.
You can now write a short brief and set up a project folder where every clip is easy to find.

check.q: Which of these belongs in a video brief?
options: Where the video will play and how long it should be
A list of every app you own
check.why: Where it plays and how long it is shape every editing choice that follows.

check.q: Your phone holds the only copy of a client's clips. What do you do first?
options: Delete the clips you don't like
Post the clips so they are saved online
Copy them to a second place such as a USB drive or cloud storage
check.why: A backup in a second place means a broken phone or a deleted file does not lose the job.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Set up the project: shape, size and speed
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the aspect ratio, resolution and frame rate for a project before you edit.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short brief and a set of raw clips, you will organize the footage in a named project folder and set the project's aspect ratio and frame rate to match where the video will play, with every clip easy to find and no clip stretched or cropped by mistake.
Before you edit, tell the editor the shape and size of the finished video. Aspect ratio is the shape. Wide 16:9 fits YouTube, laptops and TVs. Tall 9:16 fits phone apps like TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts. Square 1:1 fits some feeds. Choose the shape from your brief.
Resolution is how many dots (pixels) make up the picture. 1920 by 1080, often called 1080p or Full HD, is a safe choice for most work. For a tall video it is 1080 wide by 1920 high.
Frame rate is how many still pictures play each second, written as fps. Common rates are 24, 30 and 60. Set the project to the rate most of your clips were filmed at. You can see a clip's details in the editor or in the file's information on your computer or phone.
If the shape is wrong, the editor will add black bars or cut off the sides. If you mix up frame rates, motion can look jumpy. Setting these first saves a lot of fixing later.
Step by step:
- Read the brief: where will the video play?
- Pick the shape: 16:9 wide, 9:16 tall or 1:1 square.
- Pick the size: 1920 x 1080 wide, or 1080 x 1920 tall.
- Check the frame rate of your clips and set the project to match.
- Start the project and import your clips.
Words to know:
- Aspect ratio: the shape of the video, written as width to height, such as 16:9 (wide) or 9:16 (tall).
- Resolution: how many pixels make up the picture, such as 1920 x 1080.
- Pixel: one tiny dot of color on a screen.
- Frame rate (fps): how many still pictures play each second, such as 24, 30 or 60.
- Import: bring your clips into the editing program.
Official sources:
- Blackmagic Design: DaVinci Resolve (free version for Mac, Windows and Linux)
- Microsoft Clipchamp: plans, including the free plan
Try it now: Open a free editor: DaVinci Resolve or Clipchamp on a computer, or CapCut or your phone's built-in editor on a phone. Look up the frame rate of three of your clips. Start a new project with the shape and frame rate your brief needs, and import your clips.
You can now set up a project with the right shape, size and frame rate for where the video will play.

check.q: Your brief says the video will be an Instagram Reel. Which shape do you choose?
check.why: Reels, TikTok and Shorts play tall on a phone, so 9:16 fills the screen.

check.q: Most of your clips were filmed at 30 fps. What frame rate should the project use?
options: 60 fps, because higher is always better
Any rate; it makes no difference
check.why: Matching the rate of most of your clips keeps motion smooth.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Build a rough cut on the timeline
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Trim, split and order clips on the timeline into a story that fits the target length.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free video editor, you will build a rough cut by trimming, splitting and ordering clips on the timeline into a beginning, middle and end, that tells the brief's story in the target length with no dead time.
The timeline is the strip where you lay clips in order, left to right. The playhead is the line that shows where you are. A rough cut is your first full version: the right clips, in the right order, at about the right length. It does not need to be pretty yet.
Build it in three parts. The beginning grabs attention in the first few seconds. The middle shows the main message. The end tells the viewer what to do or remember. For a bakery: fresh bread coming out of the oven, the owner saying why she started, then the shop's sign and hours.
Two tools do most of the work. Trim cuts the start or end off a clip. Split cuts one clip into two at the playhead, so you can remove a middle part. Start each shot right before the action and end it right after. Remove dead time: waiting, looking at the camera, "um" and long pauses.
Watch the whole rough cut from the start. If it is longer than the brief allows, remove whole shots before you shorten good ones. Save often, and save a copy with a version number (v1, v2) before big changes.
Step by step:
- Drag your best clips to the timeline in story order: beginning, middle, end.
- Trim the start and end of each clip so it starts just before the action.
- Split clips to remove pauses, mistakes and dead time.
- Watch from the start and check the length against the brief.
- Remove whole weak shots if it is too long.
- Save as v1.
Words to know:
- Timeline: the strip in an editor where clips are placed in order, left to right.
- Playhead: the line on the timeline that shows the moment you are viewing.
- Trim: shorten a clip by cutting its start or end.
- Split: cut one clip into two pieces at the playhead.
- Rough cut: the first full version of an edit, with the right clips in order but not yet polished.
- Dead time: parts where nothing useful happens, such as waiting or long pauses.
Try it now: In your project, build a rough cut of your final-task video. Put clips in beginning-middle-end order, trim each one, split out at least two pauses or mistakes, and get within 10 seconds of your target length. Save it as v1 and write down its length.
You can now build a rough cut that tells a story in the target length with no dead time.

check.q: You need to remove a long pause from the middle of an interview clip. Which tool do you use?
options: Split the clip at both ends of the pause and delete the middle
check.why: Splitting at both ends of the pause lets you lift out just the middle part.

check.q: Your rough cut is 20 seconds too long. What do you try first?
options: Make every clip one second shorter
check.why: Removing weak shots keeps the strong ones whole and the story clear.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Smooth the edit with B-roll and better cuts
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Add B-roll, a cutaway and an L-cut or J-cut to smooth your rough cut.
This lesson builds toward: Given a rough cut, you will add B-roll, cutaways and simple transitions to hide jumps and keep the video moving, using no more than one or two kinds of transition.
When you cut out part of an interview, the face jumps. This is called a jump cut. Editors hide it with B-roll: shots that show what the person is talking about. A coach talks about practice; we see players running drills. The voice keeps going while the picture changes.
A cutaway is a short shot of something nearby, such as hands, a crowd or a scoreboard, placed between two shots of the same thing. Mix wide, medium and close-up shots so the viewer sees the place, the people and the details.
Two pro tricks are easy. In an L-cut, the picture changes to the next shot while the sound from the first shot keeps playing. In a J-cut, you hear the next shot before you see it. Both make the edit feel smooth and natural. Most editors let you unlink or detach the sound from the picture to do this.
Go easy on transitions. A plain cut is used most of the time by professionals. Use one or two simple transitions, such as a short fade at the start and end. Many flashy wipes and spins make a video look like a beginner made it.
Step by step:
- Watch your rough cut and mark every jump cut.
- Place B-roll on the track above the interview to cover each jump.
- Add at least one cutaway (hands, crowd, sign, scoreboard).
- Try one L-cut or J-cut by unlinking sound from picture.
- Use plain cuts, with at most one or two simple transitions.
- Save as v2.
Words to know:
- B-roll: extra shots that show what someone is talking about, placed over their voice.
- Jump cut: a sudden jump in the picture when part of a shot is cut out.
- Cutaway: a short shot of something nearby placed between two shots of the same subject.
- L-cut and J-cut: edits where the sound and picture change at different moments, so the cut feels smooth.
- Transition: an effect between two clips, such as a fade.
Try it now: Open your v1. Cover every jump cut with B-roll, add at least one cutaway, and make one L-cut or J-cut. Remove any flashy transitions so you use no more than two kinds. Save as v2 and watch v1 and v2 side by side.
You can now use B-roll, cutaways and L-cuts or J-cuts to make an edit smooth and easy to watch.

check.q: An interview has a jump cut where you removed a sentence. How do you hide it?
options: Place B-roll over the jump while the voice keeps playing
check.why: B-roll covers the jump in the picture while the speech keeps flowing.

check.q: You hear the crowd cheering before the picture cuts to the crowd. What is this called?
check.why: In a J-cut the sound of the next shot starts before its picture.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Fix the sound, add music and captions
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Balance voice and music levels, add music you have permission to use, and add accurate captions.
This lesson builds toward: Given a cut with speech and music, you will balance the sound levels and add accurate captions and on-screen text, so every word can be heard and read, the meter never hits the top, and all music is used with permission.
Viewers forgive a so-so picture but not bad sound. Use the audio meter: it shows how loud the sound is. If it reaches the top and turns red, the sound will crackle. A common target is to have voices peak around -6 on the meter, with music much lower under speech, and nothing hitting 0.
Use only music you are allowed to use: music you made, music with written permission, or the free library in your editor or platform, following its rules. The YouTube Audio Library offers music for YouTube videos; some tracks require you to credit the artist. Giving credit alone does not give you permission to use someone else's song, and there is no safe number of seconds.
Many people watch with the sound off, and captions also help viewers who are deaf or hard of hearing. Most editors can make automatic captions. Always read them and fix every mistake, especially names, places and numbers.
Add on-screen text with care: a short title, a person's name and role the first time they speak, and a final card with the message or call to action. Use large, plain letters and keep text away from the edges, where apps put their buttons.
Step by step:
- Play the edit and watch the audio meter.
- Lower any clip that turns red; raise voices that are too quiet.
- Add music you may use and lower it under speech.
- Turn on automatic captions, then read and fix every word.
- Add a title, a name label and an end card in large, plain letters.
- Save as v3.
Words to know:
- Audio meter: the bar that shows how loud the sound is.
- Clipping: crackling sound caused when the level hits the top of the meter.
- Royalty-free: music you can use without paying each time it plays, under the library's rules; it still has rules.
- Captions: the spoken words shown as text on screen.
- Call to action: what you want the viewer to do next, such as "Visit us Saturday".
Official sources:
- U.S. Copyright Office: Fair use FAQ
- YouTube Help: Use music and sound effects from the Audio Library
Try it now: Open your v2. Watch the meter and fix any clip that turns red. Add music you are allowed to use and lower it under speech. Turn on automatic captions and fix every mistake. Add a title, one name label and an end card. Save as v3, then watch it once with the sound off to check that the captions tell the story.
You can now balance sound levels, add music the right way and add captions and text people can read.

check.q: The audio meter turns red at the top when the coach shouts. What do you do?
options: Raise the volume of that clip
Lower that clip's level so it stays out of the red
check.why: Red at the top means clipping; lowering the level stops the crackle.

check.q: A client wants a popular hit song in their ad. You have no permission. What is true?
options: It is fine if you use only 10 seconds
Giving the artist credit makes it legal
Ads can use any song on the radio
You need permission, or use music from a library under its rules
check.why: There is no safe number of seconds and credit is not permission, so get permission or use licensed library music.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Export, review and build your portfolio
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Export a finished video, check it against the brief and write a portfolio note.
This lesson builds toward: Given a finished edit, you will export the video with settings that fit the platform, review it against the brief and write a short portfolio note, so the file plays correctly on the first try and the note names the brief, your role and your tools.
Exporting turns your project into one video file. For most online use, choose an MP4 file with H.264 video at the same shape, size and frame rate as your project. Name the file clearly, like "bakery-promo-v3-9x16.mp4", and save it in your exports folder. In DaVinci Resolve this happens on the page called Deliver; other editors use a button such as Export or Save.
Never send a file you have not watched. Play the exported file from start to end on the device where it will be seen. Check the brief: right length, right shape, one clear message, clean sound, correct captions and names. Then send it, ask for feedback, and make changes in a new version. Clients often ask for changes; that is a normal part of the job.
Your portfolio is a small collection of your best work. Put the video online where you are allowed to (with permission from the client and everyone in it) and write a short note: the brief, what you did, the tools you used and the result. Employers hiring junior editors, social media assistants and content creators often ask for samples like this.
Credentials can help later. Certiport, a Pearson VUE business, delivers the Adobe Certified Professional exam in Digital Video Using Adobe Premiere. Blackmagic Design offers training and online exams to become a certified DaVinci Resolve editor. Check each official page for the current requirements and costs. This course prepares you to keep learning; it does not grant either credential.
Step by step:
- Export an MP4 (H.264) at the project's shape, size and frame rate.
- Name the file clearly and save it in your exports folder.
- Watch the whole file on the device where it will play.
- Check it against every line of the brief.
- Send it, get feedback and make changes in a new version.
- Write a portfolio note: brief, your role, tools, result.
Words to know:
- Export: turn your edit into one finished video file.
- MP4 and H.264: a common file type and video format that plays on most phones, computers and websites.
- Portfolio: a small collection of your best work to show employers or clients.
- Revision: a change a client asks for after seeing a version.
- Credential: proof from a recognized organization that you passed a test of your skills.
Official sources:
- Certiport: Adobe Certified Professional exams
- Blackmagic Design: DaVinci Resolve training and certification
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Film and Video Editors and Camera Operators
Try it now: Final task: export your v3 as an MP4 in the right shape, name it clearly and watch it on the device where it will play. Check it against your brief and fix anything that does not match. Then write your portfolio note in four lines: the brief, what you did, the tools you used and the result.
You can now export a finished video, check it against a brief and present it as a portfolio piece.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Organized and set up Clips are scattered or the shape does not match the platform (black bars or cut-off sides). A named project folder with inside folders, a backup, and the project shape and frame rate match the brief. Best clips are renamed and the learner can explain why they chose the shape and frame rate. Story and length Clips are out of order, have dead time, or the video is far off the target length. Clear beginning, middle and end; no dead time; within 5 seconds of the target length. The first few seconds grab attention and every shot earns its place. Smooth editing Jump cuts are visible or many flashy transitions are used. B-roll or cutaways hide the jumps; no more than two kinds of transition. Includes a clean L-cut or J-cut and a good mix of wide, medium and close-up shots. Sound and captions Sound crackles or is hard to hear, captions have mistakes, or music has no permission. Clear voices, music under speech, accurate captions, and only music the learner may use. Name labels and an end card are clear on a phone, and music credits are given where the library requires it. Delivered and presented The file is misnamed, does not play, or the portfolio note is missing. A clearly named MP4 that plays on the target device, checked against the brief, with a four-line portfolio note. The learner got feedback and delivered a revised version, and the note says what changed. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part, export a new version and try again.

check.q: Which file name is best for the finished video?
check.why: It says the job, the version and the shape, so nobody sends the wrong file.

check.q: You just exported the video. What do you do before sending it?
options: Send it right away to save time
Delete the project to save space
Watch the whole file on the device where it will play and check it against the brief
check.why: Watching the real file catches errors before the client sees them.
